- Bundibugyo variant Ebola virus in the Democratic Republic of the Congo has caused a dramatic outbreak: 1,521 deaths and 3,442 confirmed infections since late April, yielding a case fatality rate of 44%. Transmission sources are unclear for most new patients, and contact tracing is insufficient, hindering containment. The outbreak has spread to five provinces, including areas along the border with South Sudan; the WHO declared a Public Health Emergency of International Concern in mid-May. Declared May 15, the outbreak is linked to Bundibugyo ebolavirus, for which there are no vaccines or approved treatments. It is the fastest-growing outbreak on record, concentrated mainly in Ituri province (about 90% of cases) with confirmed infections in five other provinces, including Kisangani. Uganda has declared itself Ebola-free after its last patient recovered in mid-June. article.articleHeadline: Dengue Deaths Remain High, Indonesia Targets Zero Deaths by 2030.
article.articleSummary: Indonesia continues to bear one of the world's highest dengue burdens, reporting over 257,000 dengue cases and more than 1,400 deaths in 2024. To reach zero dengue deaths by 2030, the Ministry of Health and the World Mosquito Program (WMP) signed a Memorandum of Understanding to strengthen dengue control, including the strategic use of Wolbachia-infected Aedes aegypti to reduce transmission. Wolbachia is a natural bacterium shown to suppress dengue in mosquitoes; a randomized trial in Yogyakarta, published in The New England Journal of Medicine (June 2021), linked Wolbachia deployment to a 77% reduction in dengue cases and an 86% reduction in related hospitalizations. The effort forms part of a broader approach—surveillance, early detection, case management, community engagement, and vector control—with pilot Wolbachia programs in Bandung, Semarang, Bontang, Kupang, and Jakarta Barat.

article.articleHeadline: Newcastle disease has been a major problem for a hundred years | Our Livestock - All about raising farm animals.
article.articleSummary: Newcastle disease (ND), first scientifically described in Java, Indonesia in 1926, remains a major threat to poultry. At Ceva seminar in Bogor, West Java, scientists and policymakers reflected on a century of ND, its challenges, and future directions. In Indonesia, ND outbreaks persist in at least 15 provinces, fueled by smallholder farming, weak biosecurity, poverty, and rapid poultry movements; underreporting impedes rapid response. Vaccination is central to control, supported by a national lab network and animal-health digital information system, and Indonesia now manufactures over a billion vaccine doses annually, including vaccines based on local isolates, with exports. In the UK, Weybridge Pirbright Institute researchers clarified ND's origin as a filterable virus, enabling vaccines via embryonated eggs and electron microscopy. The 1970s shift from culling to vaccination reduced UK outbreaks, but reintroductions occur through imported products, captive birds, and wild pigeons. Genomic diversity drives a decade-long push for a unified classification framework.

article.articleHeadline: Era of industrial poultry farming: Large-scale farms accelerate the spread of bacteria that cause diarrhea - Tech SME
article.articleSummary: Industrial poultry farming accelerates spread of Campylobacter, the leading cause of bacterial gastroenteritis, according to a Oxford University study in PNAS. Concentrating billions of chickens in intensive farms creates a large, persistent reservoir that facilitates inter-host transmission and evolution. Global poultry numbers have surged since the 1960s to about 31 billion birds, ~70% of all birds by mass; China, the United States, and Brazil are major producers, together near half of world production. Genomes from 2,747 Campylobacter isolates across 30 countries (1979–2024) reveal mutations improving stress tolerance, nutrient uptake, and environmental movement; antibiotic resistance is increasing, complicating treatment. In Oxfordshire, up to 80% of human campylobacteriosis cases are linked to poultry consumption. Slovakia recorded 4,961 campylobacteriosis cases in 2020; ongoing intensive poultry production and imports; 2025 avian influenza outbreak heightened biosecurity, while Salmonella remains a constant risk; proper hand hygiene remains critical.

article.articleHeadline: Case of spotted fever reinforces the importance of tick prevention - learn how to protect your pet and your family - Portal Pet News
article.articleSummary: Fatal Brazilian spotted fever case in São Paulo state (São Bernardo do Campo) underscores tick prevention for pets and families. Transmitted by infected ticks, the disease highlights that urban green spaces and homes can harbor vectors, with dogs and cats acting as hosts to transport ticks into households. While pets do not directly transmit the illness to people, ticks also carry canine diseases such as ehrlichiosis, babesiosis, and anaplasmosis, potentially causing anemia and immune suppression if untreated. Zoetis veterinarian Paula Pinheiro offers five recommendations: (1) start tick prevention year-round; (2) risk exists in urban areas; (3) inspect pets after outdoor activity, especially ears, neck, between toes, and abdomen; (4) protect the environment alongside the animal; (5) consult a veterinarian to choose the best prevention. Products cited include Simparic Trio®, protecting against Amblyomma cajennense s.l. and other parasites for up to 35 days, and EctoFend® collar, offering months of protection against ticks, fleas, leishmaniasis vector, and related parasites.

article.articleHeadline: A recurring risk: just like Zika, the Oropouche virus can also affect the brains of fetuses.
article.articleSummary: Oropouche virus expanded in Brazil in 2024, with nearly 14,000 confirmed cases, and sustained circulation across all five regions in 2025, accompanied by deaths and vertical transmission, including abortions, fetal deaths, and newborns with microcephaly. Researchers used human brain organoids to study infection, exposing neural progenitor cells to two strains: BeAn19991 (Amazonas, 1960) and RJ/LVM-2024 (Rio de Janeiro, 2024). Both infected neural stem cells; BeAn19991 infected ~87% of cells, RJ variant slightly lower. Transcriptomics showed 657 differential genes: proliferative neural stem cell genes down, inflammatory, viral replication, and apoptosis genes up. In organoids infected at ~30 days, growth slowed, borders irregular, structure disrupted; virus targeted ventricular zones with reduced Ki67-positive proliferating cells. Findings provide a possible mechanism for fetal brain impact, echoing Zika.

article.articleHeadline: The Biblical Disease Reappears: What Leprosy Is, How It Spreads, What Its Symptoms Are, and Who It Is Affecting.
article.articleSummary: Leprosy (Hansen's disease), caused by Mycobacterium leprae, has re-emerged with rising cases in the United States. Globally, about 200,000 new cases are detected annually, with most occurring in India, Brazil, and Indonesia, and active transmission in more than 120 countries. In the United States, increases are reported in southern states like Florida, Texas, and Louisiana, though overall risk remains low. Transmission requires prolonged close contact with an untreated case through droplets from the nose or mouth; casual contact is not highly contagious. Symptoms may appear 2–20 years after exposure and include skin patches with altered sensation, numbness in hands/feet, tingling, muscle weakness, thickened nerves, non-healing ulcers, and vision problems in advanced disease. Leprosy is curable with multidrug therapy, provided free by the WHO; early treatment prevents nerve damage and stops transmission.

article.articleHeadline: Rabies advances in production animals, and Santa Catarina already has 27 cases in 2026.
article.articleSummary: Two confirmed rabies cases in production animals in Itapiranga, western Santa Catarina, raise the state's 2026 total to 27, with a third case under investigation. Other Santa Catarina municipalities reporting production-animal rabies in 2026 include Gravatal, Apiúna, Pescaria Brava, Orleans, Angelina, Chapecó, São Francisco do Sul, Indaial, Major Gercino, Bocaina do Sul, São José do Cedro, Criciúma and Caçador, reflecting both the Southern region and Grande Oeste. In 2025 SC recorded 47 herbivore cases and 2024 had 67. The hematophagous bat Desmodus rotundus is the main transmitter, attacking livestock at night and spreading the virus via saliva. Producers should report frequent bat attacks or possible roosts to enable epidemiological investigation and control. Vaccination for cattle and horses aged ≥3 months is advised in identified foci and surrounding areas; schedule: initial dose, booster at 30 days, and renewals every 180 days, with vaccination voluntary rather than state-mandated.

article.articleHeadline: Sesau guides the public on Hand, Foot and Mouth Disease.
article.articleSummary: Hand, Foot and Mouth Disease (HFMD) awareness campaign by Alagoinhas’ Sesau, Brazil, educates the public on HFMD care. HFMD is highly contagious, caused by enteroviruses (notably Coxsackieviruses), affecting mainly children under five and infants. Transmission occurs via direct contact or contaminated objects, making rapid recognition crucial to prevent daycare and school outbreaks. Incubation is 3–7 days; illness lasts 7–10 days. Common symptoms include fever, sore throat, malaise, loss of appetite, painful mouth ulcers, and small blisters or red spots on the palms and soles, possibly on buttocks, legs, or genital area. No vaccine exists; prevention relies on strict hygiene and respiratory etiquette: frequent handwashing with soap or 70% alcohol, do not share cups, utensils, pacifiers, bottles, towels, or toys; clean shared surfaces. Sick children should stay home until fever and active lesions resolve and medical clearance is obtained. Treatment is symptomatic: rest, fluids, soft foods, and prescribed analgesics.

article.articleHeadline: What is mpox, the disease for which four cases were reported in the province, and how is it transmitted?
article.articleSummary: Mpox (formerly monkeypox) is caused by mpox virus. The virus was discovered in 1958 in monkeys in Denmark and the first human cases were reported 12 years later in the Democratic Republic of the Congo. The World Health Organization declared a public health emergency of international concern amid a global outbreak. In this report, four cases were reported in the province. Symptoms affect about 70% with fever, fatigue, sore throat, muscle or head pain; more than 70% develop an anogenital rash; roughly 13% experience complications. Transmission occurs mainly through close physical contact with skin lesions, mucous membranes, or bodily fluids, or via contaminated materials/textiles; sexual contact is a high-risk context. It can spread through respiratory droplets but this is far less common, and overall population transmission is considered low.

article.articleHeadline: WHO Weekly Situation Update on Ongoing Health Emergency Events in South Sudan - Week #30, Date: 20-26 Jul 2026 - South Sudan
article.articleSummary: DR Congo reports 3,200 Ebola virus disease (EVD) cases and 1,405 deaths (CFR 43.9%) in 47 health zones; Uganda declares the end of its 2026 Ebola outbreak on 28 July, leaving DRC the only country with active transmission. South Sudan remains in EVD/BVD preparedness; national readiness 65%, while subnational readiness lags. Cholera rises to 210 new cases; OCV mop-up continues in Mayom, Leer and Rubkona. Polio detects two isolates (cVDPV1 Nasir, cVDPV2 Tonj South); measles remains limited with 4 new cases. Malaria totals 57,303, 32.3% below 2025. Jonglei and Akobo remain critical (GAM 22.3%, IPC Phase 5 in several counties); fresh clash in Uror on 26 July. Priority actions: sustain OCV mop-up, restore routine immunization in Akobo (0%), Nyirol (25%), Uror (55%), support solar refrigerators, catch-up campaigns; IPV intensification and SNID (25–28 Aug); scale Jonglei nutrition response and conduct IRNA assessments in Walgak & Waat first week of August.

article.articleHeadline: DRC: four cases of poliovirus variants confirmed in Maniema Province in the first quarter of 2026.
article.articleSummary: Four cases of poliovirus variant type 2 (cVDPV2) were confirmed in Maniema province, DRC, from January to March 2026, with two cases in each health zone (Kunda and Kampene), signaling ongoing transmission despite the country being polio-free since 2011. In the first 12 weeks of 2026, 745 acute flaccid paralysis (AFP) cases were reported; the national non-polio AFP rate is 4.7, above the surveillance threshold, though several provinces (e.g., Sud-Kivu, Nord-Kivu, Ituri, Kinshasa, Kwango, Sud-Ubangi, Lomami) lag behind. Vaccination coverage among targeted children stands at 85.7%, but 3.9% are zero-dose and 11.6% have unknown vaccination status, raising transmission risk. Campaigns occurred in Equateur, Tshuapa, and Maniema, with satisfactory LQAS quality results in targeted zones. Authorities aim to intensify vaccination in high zero-dose areas, strengthen epidemiological and environmental surveillance, and improve sample transport to laboratories to interrupt cVDPV2 transmission by end-2026.

article.articleHeadline: Diary from the Ebola mission: This doctor fought one of the world's deadliest epidemics.
article.articleSummary: MSF doctor recounts a 2026 Ebola deployment, following 2014 West Africa and later DRC outbreaks. After a briefing in Brussels, he travels from Berlin to Kigali, Rwanda, then crosses to the DR Congo border at Rusizi under M23 control. In Lwiro, 40 kilometers north of Bukavu, MSF has converted a small hospital into a 35-bed Ebola treatment center. As medical team leader, he oversees care quality, conducts staff trainings, and accompanies rounds. A high-risk ward is separated by a barrier; a nearby terrace with orange fencing allows eye-to-eye contact between patients, relatives, and psychologists while preventing transmission. Community trust is fragile amid previous violence and arson against Ebola facilities in eastern DR Congo. The “no touch” policy prohibits skin contact and shared objects to limit body-fluid spread, as the team of six prepares for roughly four weeks of duty and Bundibugyo virus exposure with its lower mortality.

article.articleHeadline: DRC: Nearly 12 million people live with viral hepatitis, according to the PNLHV.
article.articleSummary: World Hepatitis Day on July 28 drew attention to viral hepatitis in the Democratic Republic of Congo (DRC). In Kinshasa, the National Program for the Fight against Viral Hepatitis (PNLHV) warned that prevalence remains high despite government efforts. Dr. Pascal Tshamala, PNLHV director, cited global figures of about 350 million people living with viral hepatitis; in the DRC, estimates range from 3% to 10% of the population, roughly 12 million people—the size of Kinshasa. The aim is hepatitis elimination by 2030 and to prevent cirrhosis and liver cancer. The World Health Organization urged improved access to screening and treatment, noting many infections are und diagnosed and that services remain unequal, especially for the disadvantaged. Experts called for integrating prevention, screening, and treatment into primary health care and continued investment in diagnostics and therapies, including hepatitis B and hepatitis D co-infection. 2026 theme: 'Hepatitis: understand the disease to defeat it.'

article.articleHeadline: On a mission to end malaria in Zambia
article.articleSummary: Malaria eradication efforts in Zambia show progress. In Central Province and across 10 districts in two provinces, the Partners for a Malaria-Free Zambia program trained 2,500 CHWs who test and treat malaria near homes, reaching 1.25 million people with testing and treatment. CHWs detected 58% of confirmed cases and treated 97.5% of those; 2.5% were referred to facilities. Malaria incidence declined from 279 to 213 per 1,000 people between 2021 and 2025. The $6 million Programs of Scale grant (2021) funded Rotary International’s $2 million to Partners for a Malaria-Free Zambia, with World Vision U.S. and the Gates Foundation providing $2 million each. The program (2021–24) has scaled into Rotary Healthy Communities Challenge (2024–27), expanding to DRC, Mozambique, Nigeria, and Zambia. World Malaria Day events in Lusaka highlighted progress, with Chief Chamuka supporting the campaign. Two years after grant end, 94% of CHW roles remain filled as of 2026.

article.articleHeadline: EXCLUSIVE: Congo's Ebola epidemic started at least 4 months before it was detected
article.articleSummary: Ebola virus disease outbreak in the Democratic Republic of the Congo’s Ituri province, centered in Mongbwalu, appears to have started in January, with a formal declaration by Kinshasa on 15 May. An unpublished analysis based on interviews with about 100 residents, nurses, and community leaders traces a transmission chain from a 50-year-old woman who died January 25 after vomiting blood; relatives followed, triggering a cluster and multiple burials. By May 15, more than 500 suspected cases had been identified since mid-January, and the epidemic has since reached about 3,360 cases with 1,487 deaths, threatening to become the second-largest on record. Front-line workers bore a heavy toll: 13 died, 42 fell ill but recovered; health facilities closed at times and Mongbwalu’s cemetery was overwhelmed. Genomic analyses from Bunia support January (or possibly mid-March) origins, underscoring surveillance gaps before Kinshasa’s alert.

article.articleHeadline: The hidden cost of crash dieting: Why doctors are seeing more TB cases in young adults - India TV News
article.articleSummary: As of 2026-07-30, crash dieting is linked to rising tuberculosis (TB) in young adults in India. At Fortis Hospital Mulund, Mumbai, Dr. Anita Mathew reports more patients with rapid weight loss and poor nutrition presenting with TB. In one case, a 30-year-old man with obesity and diabetes undertook a restrictive ketogenic-style diet and, though admitted for dengue fever, imaging revealed pulmonary TB, suggesting latent TB activation due to immune/metabolic compromise. In another, a 16-year-old girl subjected to body shaming restricted intake and lost 15–16 kg over months, developing persistent fever; TB was confirmed by biopsy, and she recovered after about four months of anti-TB therapy. The piece urges clinicians to consider TB with persistent fever during monsoon and promotes balanced nutrition, gradual weight loss, regular exercise, and medical supervision when dieting.

article.articleHeadline: Flu on the rise in Ernakulam district; July sees 989 cases
article.articleSummary: In Ernakulam district, Kerala, influenza cases surged in July 2026 to 989, up from 252 in June, with both influenza A and H1N1 involved. article.articleHeadline: Monsoon Diseases: The risk of these illnesses increases during Sawan; learn the causes and easy preventive measures.
article.articleSummary: During the Sawan monsoon in Noida, humidity and waterlogging raise the risk of viral infections, gastrointestinal diseases, fungal infections, and mosquito-borne illnesses, driven by contaminated drinking water and stagnant water that boosts mosquitoes. Sharda Hospital's internal medicine expert Dr. Shrey Srivastav notes that most illnesses arise from contaminated food, polluted water, and mosquito exposure, making prevention the biggest challenge. The article highlights the causes and outlines simple preventive measures (Sawan Health Tips) to counter these risks during the monsoon season, emphasizing practical steps readers can take to reduce exposure. It links seasonal climate to common health issues and stresses awareness during Sawan.

article.articleHeadline: Ranchi Health Alert: In the monsoon, infections are spreading from food sold openly in the streets; cases of food poisoning have increased in hospitals.
article.articleSummary: Ranchi, Jharkhand: Monsoon-related infections are rising from street foods sold openly. In the past weeks, outpatient visits at RIMS (Rajendra Institute of Medical Sciences) and Sadar Hospital, along with private hospitals, show about a 25% jump in cases of vomiting, diarrhea, fever, food poisoning, typhoid, and jaundice compared with normal days. Some patients are gravely ill and require admission; a number have been moved to neurology and critical care units. Doctors say bacteria and viruses proliferate in rain, with contaminated water, reused oil, open-air foods, flies, and inadequate hygiene driving transmission. Street stalls in Kokar, Lalpur, Main Road, Circular Road, Ratu Road, Doranda, Morhabadi sell golgappas, chaat, chole-bhature, dhoska, pav bhaji, tikki, samosa, jalebi. Precautions: eat only fresh, hot foods from clean establishments; drink bottled or boiled water; avoid cut fruits and open salads, especially for children, elderly, and ill individuals.

article.articleHeadline: Persistently red eye turned out to be an extremely rare fungal infection: Doctors save patient's vision after year-long treatment
article.articleSummary: Isolated orbital histoplasmosis, a rare fungal infection of the tissues around the eye, was diagnosed and treated in an immunocompetent patient at Artemis Hospitals, India. The presenting complaint was a persistently red eye with eye discomfort that did not respond to standard therapies. Histoplasma capsulatum, typically associated with pulmonary disease, can arise in soil contaminated with bird or bat excreta; orbital involvement in an otherwise healthy individual is exceedingly rare. Diagnosis was confirmed by tissue biopsy after unresponsiveness to conventional treatment. The patient received antifungal therapy guided by the infectious diseases team, with drug selection, dosing, and duration tailored to clinical response due to limited ocular penetration and lack of standard guidelines. Treatment continued for nearly a year, culminating in resolution of symptoms and maintained vision. The case underscores the value of early biopsy and a multidisciplinary approach when orbital infections mimic other conditions.

article.articleHeadline: Chaibasa News: Mosquito proliferation has increased in Guva, Kiriburu, and Barajamda; malaria threat rising.
article.articleSummary: Mosquito proliferation has surged in Guva, Kiriburu, and Barajamda, elevating malaria risk, according to Chaibasa News (Published July 30, 2026). Local residents say cell management previously conducted regular vector-control with mosquito repellents and fogging, which largely kept numbers in check, but this year a sharp rise has been observed. Reported causes include degraded quality of mosquito-control drugs, irregular fogging, overgrown shrubs, and pervasive waterlogging. Residents urge cell management to launch aggressive fogging, spraying, and sanitation drives immediately to curb mosquitoes and prevent malaria and other seasonal illnesses. Seasonal diseases are rising in the area; Guva Cell Hospital is crowded, with beds full. Severe cases are admitted; patients with milder ailments receive primary treatment and are sent home. Without timely control, malaria and other infectious diseases are likely to increase in the coming days.

article.articleHeadline: Statewide elephantiasis; one in three laborers, those at risk should take note.
article.articleSummary: Statewide elephantiasis mortality in Thiruvananthapuram, with statewide implications, is led by laborers who account for 36.72% of deaths, per the Health Department’s 2025 occupational sector analysis. Those at risk work in muddy waters and waterlogged areas during the monsoon. Other affected groups include farming and allied workers (10.94%), domestic gardening (10.16%), construction workers (9.38%), and unskilled laborers (7.81%). Among other occupations: painter (4.69%), fishermen, cattle-rearing, and drivers (3.13% each), tile workers and masons (2.34%), plumber, security personnel, and unemployed (1.56%), and other labor categories (0.78%). Transmission occurs mainly through contact with water and soil contaminated by animals. Prophylaxis for high-risk individuals is doxycycline 200 mg weekly, as prescribed by a physician.

article.articleHeadline: Gondia News: In Darekasa, Gondia, another patient tests positive for malaria, with the number of infected reaching 55.
article.articleSummary: On 29 July 2026, in Darekasa locality of Saleksa tehsil, Gondia district, Maharashtra, malaria was confirmed in one of 135 blood samples, bringing the year's total malaria-positive cases at Darekasa Primary Health Center to 55. Of these, 46 patients have recovered after treatment, while 9 remain under care. In response to rising cases, the district health department held a meeting on 29 July with staff from Futana, Mulla, and Bharregaon PHCs in nearby Devari tehsil, covering villages Futana, Mulla, Bharregaon, and Pindkepar, to discuss control of malaria and other vector-borne diseases such as lymphatic filariasis (elephantiasis), dengue, chikungunya, and scrub typhus. District Malaria Officer Dr. Vinod Chavan participated, outlining planned surveillance and treatment activities for the area.

article.articleHeadline: To Save Cows and Buffaloes, Do This Now; Foot-and-Mouth Disease Risk Increases During the Monsoon.
article.articleSummary: Foot-and-Mouth Disease (FMD) risk rises during the monsoon in Uttarakhand's Nainital district, prompting intensified vaccination under the Foot-and-Mouth Disease Control Programme. The first phase is complete, and mop-up rounds are in progress to cover animals missed earlier. Teams vaccinate thousands of cattle and buffalo in villages such as Jyolikot, Devidhura, Mangoli, Adhauda and Khurpatal. By July 30, 2026, a total of 5,790 animals have been vaccinated: 3,684 large and 2,106 small animals. FMD is a highly contagious viral infection spread by direct contact, contaminated feed or water; rainy-season humidity enhances transmission. Symptoms include mouth ulcers, hoof lesions, high fever, lameness, and reduced feed intake. Officials urge farmers to vaccinate remaining animals and maintain hygiene: regular shed cleaning, clean dry fodder, separation of infected stock, and sanitization of bowls and equipment to curb spread and protect milk production and livelihoods.

article.articleHeadline: In Kerala, infectious disease cases have risen due to sanitation work not being carried out before the monsoon: Minister.
article.articleSummary: Kerala's health minister K. Murali Dharan said infectious disease cases rose during the monsoon because sanitation work planned since February could not be carried out. In Thiruvananthapuram on July 30, 2026, he emphasized transparency and directed the health department to publish infection and death counts on its portal. Speaking at a media workshop, he urged clear information and welcomed media scrutiny to ensure public awareness and disease control. He attributed the rise to gaps in sanitation linked to electoral timelines: after December local body elections, about 70% of members were new, delaying implementation until the assembly elections began. A high-powered committee was formed to propose immediate and long-term remedies. Short-term measures include a 'Dry Day'—Friday in schools, Saturday in offices, Sunday at homes—to reduce mosquito breeding sites via cleaning campaigns; interdepartmental coordination is being strengthened.

article.articleHeadline: COVID-19 returns to Saurashtra; first case detected in Wankaner after 13 months; Gujarat administration on alert.
article.articleSummary: COVID-19 returns to Saurashtra with a single confirmed case in Wankaner, Morbi district, after 13 months since the last case in June 2025. A woman from the Hanuman Sheri area recently traveled to Kheda district, developed fever and malaise, and tested positive. The area is barricaded and quarantined with sanitization underway. She remains stable and has been moved to the Rajkot Civil Hospital’s specialized COVID ward for intensive care; the hospital has stockpiled oxygen and medicines. Gandhinagar was informed, and Kheda district authorities have been alerted to trace exposure and test contacts. Contact tracing is ongoing; the public is advised not to panic but to take appropriate precautions. This marks the first Saurashtra COVID-19 case since June 2025, underscoring ongoing surveillance and preparedness.

article.articleHeadline: H1N1: Precautions must be observed — Kasargod District DMO
article.articleSummary: Kasargod district, Ajanur Grama Panchayat, reports the death of a 64-year-old woman due to Influenza A H1N1. The H1N1 virus, primarily associated with pigs, transmits to humans via air and droplets, with spread possible within about one meter and through contaminated surfaces. Symptoms include fever, body aches, sore throat, dry cough, fatigue, and nausea; most recover in four to five days, but severe cases can involve pneumonia or encephalitis. High-risk groups are children under five, adults over 65, pregnant women, and individuals with comorbidities or weakened immunity. Preventive measures include wearing a mask correctly, avoiding close contact with the sick, not sharing utensils, and washing hands with soap after returning home. Sick individuals should seek prompt medical care, and contacts of H1N1 patients should undergo testing at nearby health facilities.

article.articleHeadline: Waterlogging in Daulatnagar Colony disrupts daily life; risk of diseases has increased.
article.articleSummary: Daulatnagar Colony, Loni, experiences daily waterlogging after even light rainfall due to poor drainage, leaving flooded streets and blocked avenues. Residents report water-filled alleys and gutters that hinder movement, with schoolchildren most affected as belongings get wet. Prolonged stagnation fosters mosquito breeding, elevating risks of dengue, malaria, and typhoid. Complaints have been logged on the Chief Minister’s portal, but authorities have so far offered assurances without action. Municipal officials have not implemented drainage improvements, though plans include cleaning and anti-larva spraying. The situation disrupts daily life, with residents forced to wade through contaminated water and exposure to health threats. No specific case counts or fatalities are provided; the article emphasizes ongoing risk and administrative inaction in Daulatnagar Colony, Loni.

article.articleHeadline: Boy may have developed rabies after leopard attack: Officials
article.articleSummary: Rabies suspected after leopard attack in Barwani district, Madhya Pradesh near the Maharashtra border. A nine-year-old boy, Kunal, died 21 days after being attacked on July 7 by a leopard in Moharat Mal village (Bijasan area) while grazing goats; his companion Arun, 10, was injured. Both boys were treated at Sendhwa Civil Hospital and later at MY Hospital, Indore, and discharged on July 22. Health and forest officials have not yet received laboratory confirmation of rabies; the death is being investigated for possible rabies. If rabies is detected, protocol will be followed, the area sanitised, and the leopard rescued. This incident highlights a wildlife-linked potential rabies case in Barwani, with ongoing concern for public health and safety near the MP-Maharashtra border as of 30 July 2026.

article.articleHeadline: Suspected fungal infection kills 4 kids in Balaghat tribal belt
article.articleSummary: As of 30 July 2026, Jabalpur reports a suspected fungal infection killing four children in Balaghat district’s Baihar-Birsa region (Baiga community). The outbreak spans at least four villages—Bodari, Machhurda, Limhoti and Jalda—with others experiencing fever, severe body pain and skin rashes. CMHO Paresh Ulab says four children have died; several affected youngsters were admitted to the district hospital and some have been discharged after improvement. Health authorities deployed two MD physicians and two paediatricians to the affected villages to contain spread; surveillance has intensified, though the exact number of infections is still being compiled. Villagers claim higher tolls, including more than 10 affected in a village and a child in Matla in critical condition. Officials caution about healthcare access issues in remote tribal areas and urge immediate reporting of fever, rashes or severe pain.

article.articleHeadline: Diphtheria prevention campaign to begin on August 3.
article.articleSummary: Diphtheria prevention campaign will target adolescents in Banda district, India, through a school-based vaccination drive for students in Basic and Secondary Education. Between 3 and 7 August 2026, special vaccination sessions will be held in all schools, excluding Wednesday and Saturday, to administer TT/DPT vaccines to those who were missed during the April 2026 campaign. The initiative is led by Chief Medical Officer Dr. Vijendra Singh. The drive aims to shield teenagers from diphtheria, with a focus on catch-up immunization for those previously left out. No local case counts are reported in the article; the emphasis is on preventive vaccination and improving protection in the adolescent population via school-based delivery, coordinated at the district level.

article.articleHeadline: Fiji Has The World's Fastest Growing HIV Epidemic - And It Is Struggling - Health Policy Watch
article.articleSummary: Fiji faces the world’s fastest-growing HIV epidemic, with an estimated 12,000 people living with HIV in a population under 1 million. The outbreak, declared in January 2025 and initially confined to people who inject drugs, has spread to broader groups. UNAIDS estimates 1.2% HIV prevalence among 15–49-year-olds, antenatal prevalence above 2%, and in 2025 one HIV-positive child is born per week, with a monthly HIV-related child death. Over five years there is a 14-fold rise in infections, two-thirds of new diagnoses aged 20–34, and 94% of cases in the indigenous iTaukei population. Transmission is driven by shared needles for crystal meth and communal sharing practices; harm-reduction remains limited, with no sustained needle/syringe program, ARV shortages, and police crackdowns on needle access. Fiji relies on Australia, New Zealand and India for ARVs and Global Fund support, with a planned three-year transition, risking regional spillover.

article.articleHeadline: Mortality and cost of therapy of carbapenem susceptible vs resistant Gram-negative infections among hospitalised patients in India: a multicentric surveillance (2022-2025)
article.articleSummary: Multicentre observational study in India (April 2022–April 2025) across 20 tertiary care hospitals analyzes ICMR antimicrobial resistance surveillance network data to quantify mortality and cost of therapy for carbapenem-susceptible versus carbapenem-resistant Gram-negative infections. Hospitalized patients with microbiologically confirmed infections by Escherichia coli, Klebsiella pneumoniae, Acinetobacter baumannii, and Pseudomonas aeruginosa were enrolled. Mortality among carbapenem-resistant infections is compared with phenotypically susceptible infections of the same species; secondary outcomes include length of stay, total cost of therapy, and treatment patterns with ceftazidime-avibactam or polymyxin-based regimens. The study addresses the burden and resource implications of resistant Gram-negative pathogens in Indian tertiary care settings, informing therapeutic strategies and policy. Findings will contribute to understanding the differential outcomes and economic impact of resistance across major GNB species in India.

article.articleHeadline: Multiple organ dysfunction syndrome due to septic shock from biliary tract infection.
article.articleSummary: Multiple organ dysfunction syndrome from septic shock due to biliary tract infection in a 31-year-old Cambodian woman treated in Ho Chi Minh City, Vietnam. After ERCP removed a common bile duct stone, she presented with severe abdominal pain, fever, jaundice, and hypotension (70/52 mmHg). MRI showed dilated intrahepatic and extrahepatic ducts with sludge; the gallbladder contained an ~11 mm stone. She required ICU support with fluids, vasopressors, broad-spectrum antibiotics, and blood cultures. After 24 hours, she stabilized and underwent a combined procedure: ERCP stone extraction and laparoscopic cholecystectomy in a single session. Intraoperative findings included a distal CBD stone ~18 mm and a large left hepatic duct stone; stones were fragmented and removed, ducts flushed, and a stent placed. A subsequent laparoscopic cholecystectomy used a fundus-first approach due to heavy inflammation; gallbladder contained 10–12 mm stones near the neck. Postoperative recovery improved; discharge after 5 days. Clinicians highlight gallstone complications—cholangitis, sepsis, biliary obstruction—and urge early recognition of RUQ pain, fever, and jaundice.

article.articleHeadline: Six high-risk individuals developed severe disease after contracting COVID-19.
article.articleSummary: Vietnam's Ministry of Health reports rising COVID-19 and seasonal influenza activity. Seasonal influenza circulates year-round in Vietnam and rises during summer-to-autumn; COVID-19 activity is rising too. Six high-risk groups are identified: elderly; children; pregnant women; people with cardiovascular disease, chronic lung disease, diabetes, kidney disease; immunocompromised individuals; and cancer patients undergoing therapy or on immunosuppressants. High-risk individuals should adopt preventive measures to reduce hospitalization and death: masks in healthcare facilities and crowded places; hand hygiene; cover coughs and sneezes; keep living spaces ventilated; maintain good nutrition, exercise, and sleep; manage underlying diseases. Seek care for fever, cough, sore throat, runny nose, or fatigue; limit contact and avoid self-medication if symptoms persist or worsen. As of July 30, 2026, Hanoi reports three weeks of rising COVID-19 cases, 17 in the past week across 12 districts; cumulative 29 in 2026. Surveillance continues to guide response.

article.articleHeadline: A swollen, painful ear that was mistaken for a common ear infection turned out to be a highly dangerous infectious disease.
article.articleSummary: 60-year-old man in Phú Thọ Province, Vietnam, presented with a swollen, painful right parotid region initially managed as a harmless abscess. He underwent incision and drainage; pus was cultured and identified Burkholderia pseudomallei, the agent of Whitmore’s disease (melioidosis). The patient was transferred to the Infectious Diseases ward for antibiotic therapy guided by susceptibility testing and close clinical care. He has become afebrile with significant reduction of the abscess and good response to treatment. Whitmore is described as a dangerous infectious disease capable of causing bacteremia and multi-organ injury; it is endemic in tropical regions, especially Southeast Asia and northern Australia. Transmission occurs through contact with contaminated soil or water and can occur via wounds or inhalation. Early, accurate laboratory confirmation and antibiotic-guided therapy are crucial to reduce complications and mortality.

article.articleHeadline: Hyundai Bio's Jepti confirms inhibitory effect on H1N1 in human alveolar organoids - EBN News Center
article.articleSummary: Published 2026-07-30: Hyundai Biopharma's Jepti (XAFTY) niclosamide inhibited influenza A(H1N1) replication by 99.2% in human alveolar organoids derived from embryonic stem cells. Infection with A/Korea/01/09 followed by concentration-dependent treatment reduced HA mRNA from 12,858.439 to 101.692; four repeats, with a standard influenza therapy as control. Korea's National Preclinical Testing Center (KPEC) at KRIBB validated the result. The antiviral concentration matches prior COVID-19 and H1N1 animal efficacy data and Charles River respiratory-virus tests, supporting a host-cell pathway-targeted mechanism. Oral PK showed higher lung than plasma levels; NOAEL established in GLP 13-week studies, with clinical doses within this range. U.S. AIR-V basket trial for influenza, COVID-19, RSV is being prepared through UCSD's Davey Smith; Vietnam dengue Phase 2/3 continues with no SAE or drug-related discontinuations; COVID-19 results in Nature Communications bolster Jepti's potential.

article.articleHeadline: Tracheal stenosis and lung collapse after contracting tuberculosis.
article.articleSummary: Ho Chi Minh City, Vietnam: A 32-year-old woman with a history of pulmonary tuberculosis and endobronchial TB who had been declared cured six months earlier develops chest tightness and dyspnea. CT at Tam Anh General Hospital shows a 2.3 cm mid-tracheal segment with 87% stenosis and a narrowed lumen of 3.6 x 8.7 mm; the left lung is completely collapsed. Clinicians attribute the obstruction to post-tuberculous mucosal damage, cartilage necrosis, and fibrotic scarring leading to progressive tracheobronchial narrowing. After multidisciplinary discussion, surgical resection of the stenotic segment is performed using a sliding tracheoplasty technique to restore airflow. Anesthesia employs a supraglottic mask to minimize further airway injury; an end-to-end tracheal anastomosis is completed with distal tracheal intubation, and chin-to-chest fixation is applied to reduce anastomotic tension. Postoperative ICU care, pain control, and suture removal after 4 days. One week later, respiratory symptoms improve; left main bronchus obstruction will be addressed to maximize ventilation. Regular follow-up for post-TB airway scarring is advised.

article.articleHeadline: Three trucks carrying pigs blocked from entering Ho Chi Minh City; over 35 tons destroyed due to banned substances and disease.
article.articleSummary: Three trucks carrying 280 pigs totaling 35.3 tons were blocked from entering Ho Chi Minh City on July 26, with all animals subsequently destroyed under veterinary supervision after testing positive for banned substances and disease. Quick tests detected Beta-agonist additives Salbutamol and Clenbuterol in all three loads; 16 pooled blood samples from one load tested positive for African swine fever virus (ASFV). The consignments weighed 80, 115, and 85 pigs respectively; some animals died or showed weakness. On July 28–29, authorities carried out disposal to meet sanitary and environmental standards. The Ho Chi Minh City Department of Animal Husbandry and Veterinary Medicine said it would pursue enforcement against those transporting pigs with prohibited substances and increase spot checks at major entry points to prevent illicit animal movements. Earlier, 219 pigs in Dong Nai’s Tri An ward were detained after urine tests showed Salbutamol, also en route to Ho Chi Minh City.

article.articleHeadline: Ho Chi Minh City records outbreak of lumpy skin disease, strengthens disease prevention measures in the cattle herd.
article.articleSummary: An outbreak of lumpy skin disease (LSD) was detected July 7, 2026 in a four-cattle herd at ấp Định An, xã Dầu Tiếng, Bình Dương Province. A 2-month-old calf died after fever, nasal discharge and nodules. Ho Chi Minh City’s Department of Livestock Production and Veterinary Medicine coordinated with local authorities to cull the carcass, disinfect the premises, and tighten surveillance; cattle are not allowed to graze outside. Samples tested positive for LSD virus at the Central Veterinary Diagnostic and Testing Center II, marking the first LSD outbreak in Ho Chi Minh City in 2026. LSD is caused by Neethling-type virus, transmitted by biting insects and cattle movement; it is not zoonotic. Nationwide, 42 LSD outbreaks at 131 farms in 87 hamlets across 37 communes; 86 cattle affected; two outbreaks still active after 21 days. Vaccination and vector control are advised; Ho Chi Minh City offers free LSD vaccine for smallholders under 40 cattle.

article.articleHeadline: Ho Chi Minh City tightens quarantine controls, intercepts vehicles carrying nearly 200 ducks without documents.
article.articleSummary: On 30 July 2026, Ho Chi Minh City's interagency team intercepted a truck carrying 196 slaughter ducks from Đồng Nai Province into Ho Chi Minh City without a veterinary certificate. The seizure occurred at the Độc Lập–Lê Duẩn intersection along National Route 51 in Phú Mỹ Ward. The driver and consignor could not present the required animal transport health certificate; the ducks were sourced from multiple small farms in Phước Thái, Đồng Nai, for sale in HCMC. An administrative violation was issued; a 7 million VND fine was imposed, and the owner must cover sampling and disease-surveillance testing costs for re-quarantine. The birds are held under quarantine at Phú Mỹ Animal Quarantine Station while laboratory results are pending. Authorities warn of ongoing poultry-disease risks, especially avian influenza, and will intensify checks at city gateways, including nighttime hours, to prevent cross-province spread. This is the second violation of the month.

article.articleHeadline: The danger posed by Leptospira spirochetes to the human body.
article.articleSummary: Leptospira spirochete infection (leptospirosis) poses a serious health risk, rising during the rainy season in areas with poor sanitation. Reservoirs include rats, dogs, pigs, cattle, and wildlife; most carriers shed bacteria in urine, contaminating water and soil. Humans acquire infection through contact with contaminated water or mud via broken skin or mucous membranes, ingestion of contaminated food or water, or contact with infected animals. Incubation is 2–30 days (typically 7–14). Early symptoms mimic flu: fever, headache, muscle pain in calves and back, fatigue, cough, nausea, and red eyes. Without prompt treatment, severe leptospirosis can cause kidney injury, liver damage (Weil’s disease), vascular leakage with hypotension and shock, and other complications such as meningitis, myocarditis, pulmonary hemorrhage, ARDS, or GI bleeding. Early antibiotics improve outcomes; prevention includes vaccination for animals, rodent control, PPE, and avoiding contaminated water. In Long An, Vietnam, a 41-year-old man required mechanical ventilation and dialysis at People’s Hospital 115.

article.articleHeadline: Children under 2 years old with influenza B should be vigilant for the risk of severe complications.
article.articleSummary: Influenza B in Vietnam is usually mild and managed at home, but infants and young children, especially under 2 years, are at risk of severe complications. Transmission is via respiratory droplets; incubation is 1–4 days, possibly longer in immunocompromised children. Common symptoms include fever, sore throat, dry cough, headache, myalgia, fatigue, nausea, vomiting, and diarrhea; respiratory symptoms can mimic a cold. Most cases recover in 1–2 weeks, though cough and fatigue may persist >2 weeks. Severe outcomes include pneumonia (viral or bacterial superinfection), and rarely myocarditis, encephalitis, rhabdomyolysis, or multi-organ failure. High-risk groups include children under 5, especially under 2, and those with chronic conditions (immunodeficiency, liver/kidney disease, asthma, chronic lung disease, obesity). Home care emphasizes rest, fluids, fever reducers (paracetamol 10–15 mg/kg per dose; ibuprofen 6–8 mg/kg), and avoiding antibiotics; antivirals are used in select cases. A 12-year-old girl in Phú Thọ Province died after rapid influenza B progression.

article.articleHeadline: Contracting Gonorrhea after oral sex with a one-night stand.
article.articleSummary: In Hanoi, Vietnam, a single-case report documents a 30-year-old man who developed acute urethritis with burning urination and persistent yellow purulent penile discharge after oral sex with a casual partner met via Facebook. Urine PCR confirmed Neisseria gonorrhoeae infection (gonorrhea). Symptoms included foul-smelling discharge and urethral swelling, with onset following foreplay that included oral stimulation; the patient had used a condom for vaginal intercourse but not protection during oral sex, highlighting potential transmission via oro-genital contact. The patient received antibiotics per standard protocol and was advised to abstain from sex during treatment. Preventive guidance emphasized fidelity to a single partner, avoiding oral sex when oral ulcers are present, and using condoms during oral sex to reduce transmission risk. The report underscores gonorrhea as a risk from oral sex and the importance of timely medical evaluation.

article.articleHeadline: Why has the dengue fever outbreak in Vũng Áng Ward still not been brought under control?
article.articleSummary: Dengue fever outbreak in Vũng Áng Ward, Ha Tĩnh Province, Vietnam persists with 113 cases in Ky Long neighborhood as of 30 July; first case was reported on 6 April in Hop Tiến (Hợp Tiến) Hamlet, now Ky Long. Despite rapid epidemiological investigations, targeted vector control, and three rounds of wide-area insecticide spraying by Vũng Áng Health Station with Ha Tĩnh CDC support, transmission remains due to high-density migrant-worker housing, population mobility, and gaps in environmental sanitation that sustain mosquito breeding sites in water containers and waste. Public health campaigns emphasize bed nets day and night, environmental cleaning, disposal of waste, and larval-source reduction with routine door-to-door checks. Weekly cases have declined to about 1–2, but new infections continue. Since start of 2026, Ha Tĩnh Province reports 186 dengue cases (152 locally acquired, 34 imported).

article.articleHeadline: Salmonella found in a batch of chicken offal that arrived in Primorye from China.
article.articleSummary: Salmonella detected in an imported batch of frozen chicken hearts in Primorye (Primorsky Krai), Russia. Laboratory studies were conducted under a state assignment by APK Natsryba. The violation points to possible lapses in production, storage, or transportation temperature controls. The shipment was logged in the veterinary information system Vesta and sent to the Primorsky Interregional Administration for response actions. This is the first Salmonella finding in chicken byproducts in Primorye in 2026. No consumer exposure details provided; authorities will determine next steps, including regulatory actions on imports.

The Health School designation will integrate schistosomiasis education into daily health programming, promoting hygiene and healthy behaviors among students and extending to families and communities. Local education and health officials praised Chinese support for schistosomiasis control, health education, and school health work, noting progress in awareness and integrated control. Wang Jie of the Jiangsu Institute of Parasitic Disease Control called for sustaining health-education efforts via the Health School platform. The team also donated health-education materials to local authorities and Hemed Middle School.

article.articleHeadline: CMC Chairman's Debauchery: Subordinates Follow Suit as AIDS Spreads Through the Armed Forces
article.articleSummary: AIDS (HIV) spread within the Chinese military, linked to sexual networks among senior officers and military clubs. Since the 1990s, following reports of Jiang Zemin’s alleged favoritism toward Song Zuying, rumors of indiscretion circulated in PLA ranks, with naval and other service clubs becoming hubs. Figures cited include former Navy Commander Zhang Dingfan, who reportedly sought liaisons in Qingdao, Dalian and Zhanjiang, along with Gu Junshan and Wang Shouye involved in sexual/corruption misconduct. In 2005, a death from AIDS at the PLA General Hospital 301 Hospital triggered three measures by the General Logistics Department: internal control for acute infections, targeted screening within social circles, and staff education; health authorities echoed containment efforts. Military hospitals in Nanjing, Guangzhou, and Shenyang reportedly showed STD/AIDS prevalence among high-ranking cadres reaching about 20%. In 2006, Hu Jintao ordered restrictions on employing female personnel in military spaces and clubs, though enforcement was weak.

article.articleHeadline: Parasites invisible to the naked eye may be hiding in lettuce, cabbage, and strawberries that many people regularly eat!
article.articleSummary: Cyclosporiasis, caused by Cyclospora cayetanensis, is an intestinal protozoan infection acquired by ingesting mature oocysts on contaminated foods or water. The parasite commonly adheres to surfaces of raw leafy vegetables (lettuce, cabbage) and fruits (strawberries). Oocysts are 8–10 μm and invisible to the naked eye; once ingested they release sporozoites that invade intestinal cells, undergo replication, and shed infectious oocysts in stool, sustaining transmission. The global burden of foodborne cyclosporiasis has risen with expanded fresh produce trade; China has reported cases among diarrheal patients and children. Symptoms include watery diarrhea, abdominal pain, nausea/vomiting, and weight loss; severe disease can occur in the immunocompromised, elderly, and especially children under 2, potentially causing developmental delays with prolonged diarrhea. Prevention emphasizes kitchen hygiene, using separate utensils, washing produce under running water, peeling or discarding damaged areas, and thorough cooking.

High-risk groups include family members with hepatitis B or C, long-term alcohol or drug use, obesity and metabolic abnormalities. Treatment should be standardized; dispelling reliance on folk remedies and stopping meds. Some hepatitis B patients may achieve clinical cure with proper therapy, but cessation requires clinician judgment. Prevention addresses transmission, vaccination, and practical liver-care tips. article.articleHeadline: Barbecue with ice-cold beer: a 28-year-old man's vomiting and diarrhea led to collapse! Summer diarrheal illness is common—don’t ignore these warning signs.
article.articleSummary: Barbecue with ice-cold beer and a very cold air-conditioned room triggered acute gastroenteritis in a 28-year-old man in Jiangsu Province, China. After eating grilled foods and drinking iced beverages, he developed severe vomiting, watery diarrhea, and dehydration by the next dawn, leading to hospital admission at a Jiangsu provincial government hospital. A gastroenterology specialist emphasized that summer is peak season for gastrointestinal diseases due to active bacteria and viruses and irritation of the gut. In hot, humid conditions, Salmonella, Norovirus, and pathogenic Escherichia coli multiply rapidly; foods such as cooked dishes, salads, marinated meats, and seafood left at room temperature for more than two hours are at risk of contamination. Urgent-care signs include dehydration, altered mental status, very low urine output, and cold extremities. Prevention focuses on food storage limits (no more than 2 hours at room temperature), fully cooking foods, avoiding cross-contamination, good hygiene, reduced cold exposure, and not chilling the abdomen excessively.

article.articleHeadline: Industrial chicken farming accelerating spread of diarrhoea bacteria
article.articleSummary: Campylobacter, the world's leading bacterial cause of diarrhoea, is spreading faster due to industrial chicken farming, which accelerates exchange of strains between chickens and wild birds. The study analyzed nearly 2,800 genomes from chickens and wild birds across 30 countries, including the United Kingdom, United States, and China, spanning 1979–2024. Since the 1960s global chicken numbers rose seven-fold to about 27 billion birds, representing roughly 70% of all bird biomass, with intensive breeding producing “super growing” chickens slaughtered around five weeks old. Intensified farming creates a “cauldron of bacterial evolution” where strains hybridize and antimicrobial resistance traits rise, jeopardizing treatment effectiveness for campylobacter infections. Infections are commonly linked to raw chicken, with 60–80% acquired from poultry; contamination can occur via surfaces, though cooking kills pathogens.

article.articleHeadline: The Black Death turned out to be older than civilization: scientists have found the oldest traces of the plague.
article.articleSummary: Yersinia pestis (plague) traces dating up to 8,000 years ago were found in East Eurasia. Researchers reconstructed three previously unknown genomes: one in East Asia—the first prehistoric evidence of infection there—and two from Bronze Age burials in present-day Khakassia, Russia. Comparisons with known samples indicate a common ancestor about 5,300 years ago, after which lineages that would appear in northern China, Central Europe, and Scandinavia diverged within centuries, with minimal genetic differences. The study employed paleogenomics, screening roughly 1,400 samples before full-genome sequencing of the most promising specimens. High dispersal speed is implied, likely driven by migrations and trade; carriers could include humans, domestic animals, or parasites such as fleas. The pathogen’s evolution was gradual, so ancient forms could differ from the classic bubonic plague. Limitations: few complete genomes; more samples needed. Published in Nature Communications.

article.articleHeadline: African swine fever found in Finland for the first time - will stop pork exports to many countries.
article.articleSummary: First-ever African swine fever (ASF) detected in Finland, in Virolahti, eastern Finland, with dead wild boar piglets testing positive. Preliminary results indicate ASF; confirmation will come from the EU reference laboratory in Spain. Authorities instituted an immediate infection zone and are tracing spread while restricting hunting within the zone to avoid moving infected wild boars. Domestic pigs are kept on fenced areas; measures aim to contain the outbreak and limit further spread. Transmission occurs via close contact or ingestion of contaminated meat; virus persists in meat. Public advised to report dead wild boar or suspected infection to the municipal veterinarian.

article.articleHeadline: Parasite Settles in Spinal Cord for 12 Years, 55-Year-Old Man Suffers Hemiplegia
article.articleSummary: 55-year-old man from Hunan, China, with a 12-year spinal sparganosis course presenting with progressive lower-limb weakness, numbness, and urinary difficulties. History includes hydrocephalus managed by ventriculoperitoneal shunt. Initial MRI resembled a spinal tumor; serology was positive for sparganum antibodies. Although antiparasitic therapy yielded partial improvement, neurological deficits persisted. A cited 2024 case at Nanfang University Third Hospital motivated him to seek care. Multidisciplinary team performed thoracic–lumbar canal decompression and removal of the spinal lesion; intraoperative findings showed extensive parasite activity and adhesions along the spinal cord and cauda equina. Postoperative pathology and gene testing confirmed sparganosis due to Spirometra spp. infection. Postoperative motor strength in the lower limbs improved from grade 2 to 3 with better right-leg movement. Prevention emphasizes avoiding exposure to raw or undercooked frog/other meat, untreated water, and using separate cutting boards for raw and cooked foods.

article.articleHeadline: Cyclist collides with a bat, treated as a Category III rabies exposure. Why are bats special?
article.articleSummary: Rabies exposure after a bat collision prompts Category III management in Zhejiang Province, China. A cyclist was struck in the face by a bat; at Zhejiang Provincial People's Hospital, Dr. Yan Guangzhao notes that rabies is nearly 100% fatal once symptoms appear. Under the 2023 Rabies Exposure Prevention guidelines, direct bat contact qualifies as Class III exposure, requiring immediate wound care and administration of both rabies immunoglobulin and rabies vaccine, regardless of minor skin injuries. The article clarifies that mucous membrane exposure applies to parts of the mouth impacted by the bat; lip skin is not mucosal. Because bats carry higher viral loads, even a facial impact warrants full post-exposure prophylaxis. The need for tetanus vaccination should be assessed based on the wound. This case underscores bat-specific risk and the imperative of prompt prophylaxis after potential rabies exposure.

article.articleHeadline: Nipah Virus in Thailand: What to Know Before You Travel
article.articleSummary: Nipah virus in Thailand is a travel concern but warrants prudent, not panicked, conduct. Nipah is a zoonotic virus linked to fruit bats and intermediate hosts, with rapid outbreak investigations including contact tracing and reinforced hospital measures in Asia. For travelers, the overall risk to the general population remains low unless there is direct animal exposure, consumption of contaminated foods, or exposure in healthcare settings with transmission. Early symptoms resemble other infections (fever, headache, malaise, cough, fatigue) and can progress to neurological involvement. Warning signs include persistent fever, severe headache, vomiting or dizziness, confusion, somnolence, and breathing difficulties. Practical advice emphasizes basic prevention, health monitoring during travel, and seeking medical evaluation promptly if symptoms arise; keep travel itineraries handy to aid diagnosis. The article advises vigilance without alarm and encourages informed travel decisions.

article.articleHeadline: Researchers recovered smallpox DNA from two mummies in Chile.
article.articleSummary: Researchers recovered DNA of variola virus (smallpox) from two naturally mummified individuals from a southern Inca community near the Pacific coast of northern Chile, close to the Gulf of Camarones. The remains—a 30–35-year-old woman and an 18–20-year-old man—died during the early colonial period and show infection from the same viral strain. Genomic analysis places the two genomes in a now-extinct lineage of variola, evolving between strains that caused medieval European outbreaks and those dominant in later centuries. The study supports that smallpox was carried by Spaniards to the Americas after 1492, with the earliest documented American outbreak on Hispaniola in 1518, contributing to massive indigenous mortality (~90%), aiding conquest of the Aztec, Maya, and Inca realms. Evolution slowed during major colonial epidemics and resumed after the first vaccine in 1796. The last case was in Somalia in 1977; WHO declared global eradication in 1980.

article.articleHeadline: Bloc Steps Up Animal Disease Response
article.articleSummary: Foot-and-mouth disease (FMD) across Southern Africa, with Botswana and South Africa advancing a 2026–2028 joint action plan and broader regional cooperation involving Namibia, Zambia, Zimbabwe, and Lesotho under SADC. The Botswana Vaccine Institute supports vaccine supply and cross-border disease management to protect livestock and trade. The plan emphasizes improved surveillance, targeted vaccination in high-risk areas, diagnostics, and coordinated response mechanisms, recognizing that fragmented national responses are insufficient for transboundary diseases with major economic and export implications. Regional platforms and bilateral agreements underpin expanded, integrated animal health strategies, strengthening agricultural resilience and trade security across Botswana, South Africa, and neighboring nations, with intensified cross-border information sharing.

article.articleHeadline: Ghana: Hepatitis B - Ghana Cannot Afford a Silent Crisis
article.articleSummary: Ghana faces a silent hepatitis crisis: ~3 million people live with chronic hepatitis B, with <1% diagnosed and <1% of those diagnosed receiving treatment. During World Hepatitis Day, the Ghana Health Service highlighted the gap as hepatitis B deaths rose from 15,443 in 2024 to about 16,000 in 2025; hepatitis C deaths also increased. To reach WHO targets of diagnosing 90% and treating 80% by 2030, Ghana plans a nationwide birth-dose vaccination program, vaccine coverage for the third HBV dose at ~95% among infants, expanded screening, stronger surveillance, and decentralised services. Mother-to-child transmission accounts for ~95% of HBV infections; high-prevalence regions include Savannah, Northern, Upper West, and Upper East. The Technical Working Group on viral hepatitis will focus on expanding testing, improving treatment access, and monitoring progress. Public awareness and sustained investment are urged to convert words into action.

article.articleHeadline: Ghana Marks Milestones and Challenges in One Year of COVID-19 Pandemic Fund Implementation
article.articleSummary: Ghana's COVID-19 pandemic response fund, totaling GH₵X billion (≈$Y million), marks one year of implementation with three strategic pillars. CFR fell from 4.2% in 2020 to 2.1% in 2021, and testing capacity rose from 5,000 tests in early 2020 to over 20,000 per week by mid-2021. GDP contracted 6.3% in 2020 but rebounded in 2021, aided by targeted sector support. Public trust rose, with 78% of Ghanaians reporting higher compliance with safety protocols. Looking ahead, Ghana aims to expand the fund to mental health, vaccine research, and climate-resilient healthcare; it is boosting local PPE and vaccine production (e.g., Asofa) and leading ECOWAS regional procurement. The Ghana Health Pass now includes vaccination records. WHO Africa commends transparency but cautions that vaccine equity remains a challenge, noting 12% of Africans fully vaccinated by mid-2021.
